title: Hymn to the Perfection of Wisdom
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett emphasizes the importance of balancing healing and transformation in one's spiritual journey, recognizing that both are essential for growth and self-awareness. They encourage embracing nurturing and care as a vital part of the practice, rather than solely focusing on personal growth or transformation. This approach is rooted in Buddhist wisdom, particularly in the concept of prajnaparamita, which embodies the wisdom that goes beyond wisdom itself.
topics: Hymn to the Perfection of Wisdom

sentences.text: Thank you.
So many people do so much that we can have this place and do what we're doing here.
And if you think to yourself, "I'm not doing much, I just came here for some reason," that's a lot too.
So anyway, thank you.
As you might know, I spent a couple of weeks in Oregon.
Razal and I both were in Oregon, doing slightly different things.
What I was doing was a little pilgrimage, a little self-directed Zen temple tour.
The I-5 corridor in Oregon has seven Zen centers.
Actually, eight.
I missed one.
I did miss one.
I'll have to go back.
And in most of them I already knew the teacher or somebody.
So I got to have tea or dinner and spend time talking shop.
I got to talk Zen shop for many, many, many hours.
It seems to be endlessly fun for people who do this thing.
We never get tired of talking shop.
And mostly I got to see different sanghas in action and see how different people do things.
It's all recognizably Zen practice.
We teach sangha with some different arrangements.
So it was really fun, and I'll be digesting and learning from that for some time to come.
And occasionally I'll be conferring with my elders and advisors about little things we might want to adopt that I saw in other places, or be informed by.
One of the conversations, though, felt a little awkward for a minute, but then I ended up really appreciating it.
I had dinner with a colleague quite senior to me, in this hip Portland pizza place.
And he looks at me with pretty good Zen eyes and says, "What's your vow?"
I went, "Um, practice."
He had a clear sense of his own vow.
I don't know if I said a few things that were coherent to him, but later I thought about it.
And I'm also grateful that when I get tongue-tied with a teacher, I don't feel so embarrassed anymore.
I'm like, oh, well, I actually fought back a little bit.
I said, "Hey, is this dinner or dokusan?
What are we doing?"
And he said, "Oh, I just like to pry."
Then he kept at it.
"What are you doing?"
I'd say something, and he'd say, "Well, why?
What's that mean?"
It made me realize that my vow is that we can have a place where two really important things can be happening together, which I've come to think of as two paths braided together.
I call these two paths the path of healing and the path of transformation.
So we all need healing.
That's for sure.
We're all wounded and traumatized in various ways.
And this is not some new invention of trauma psychology, right?
The Buddha figured this out.
We've always known this.
To be a living person, with all of the things that entails, involves challenge, trauma, pain and disaster, with joy, love, connection, and yeah, everything.
So we definitely need healing.
I hope that our place of practice here is a place of healing, where people feel seen and heard and appreciated, and maybe appropriately left alone when that's what's needed, right?
And when they go to the teachers asking for healing and reassurance, we find some ways to support that possibility.
Largely by helping, I hope, I think, helping people see that they have all this within them.
We have what we need within us to heal.
It's not something we have to run around and get.
But we also need not just healing, because the path of healing can be limiting without the path of transformation.
The path of transformation is the path of seeing radically, seeing life and reality in a radically different way.
A way that's free, a way that's not caught by our conditioning and our preferences and our patterns.
A way that's beyond anything we can think about or figure out or talk about, but a real thing, a real feeling, a real way.
And Zen's magic has always been its incredible focus and depth in this path of transformation.
That's the gig.
And that's why Zen Buddhism caught on so strongly, amongst a small number of people but in a very strong way, when Western convert Zen Buddhists started practicing in the sixties and seventies.
But whenever I tell that story, I want to remind myself that Zen Buddhism has been here as long as Japanese immigrants have been here.
It's not an invention of the fifties or the sixties or the hippies or something like that.
But in that period, Westernized Americans started saying, "Wow, they've got something important over there.
I want to know about that."
And innovative teachers found ways to include these scruffy young Americans.
The path of transformation is about realizing in a fundamental way that actually we're not wounded after all.
The idea of woundedness is transitory and empty, and about as solid as a cloud is.
It's something, and it's powerful, but it's not solid in that way.
The path of transformation is the path of total freedom.
And those early Zen stories about people popping off into enlightenment, of course, are very exciting.
But now we know it's not just practicing really hard until you pop off into enlightenment.
It's a long journey with ups and downs and lefts and rights, and it has to be intertwined with the path of healing.
So I realize that's my hope for us, that we do both.
Transformation without healing can be harsh and unforgiving, uncompromising, and doesn't work for a lot of people.
We misinterpret it as cruel or demeaning, or it's done a little bit unskillfully, and then maybe it is cruel and demeaning.
The path of transformation is about turning our life around, seeing everything in a new way.
And for all this to work, we have to be really committed to taking responsibility for our own minds.
I think that's the essential ingredient in both paths: taking responsibility for our own minds.
It's not to say anything's our fault.
That's a different idea.
That would just be blaming ourselves.
But we recognize that we are at the crux of our life, exactly, only me, only you.
We're the only ones who can practice right here and right now.
And if we want to heal and transform, it's up to us, actually.
Luckily, there's a lot of support.
I hope there's a lot of support here and a lot of support in the universe for this.
The tricky thing is to recognize which of these paths is most helpful at any one moment.
And sometimes it's not what we think at first.
We get ruffled or frustrated or feel whatevered, fill in the blank.
Sometimes we just need somebody to apologize.
We need to explain what we need.
We need to have a process.
We need healing.
Absolutely.
Sometimes that's just continuing the same old stuff forever, right?
There never will be a time when everybody treats you the way that part of you wants to be treated.
It's never going to happen.
I was just talking to somebody about this in a long relationship, right?
So we also need to invite the possibility of transformation in that moment.
Take in this energy, this feeling.
See what it really is about and release it again.
Do I need to straighten anybody out?
Do I need to solve anything?
Do I need a process, or can I just be and feel what I feel and it's okay?
So it all gets tricky and subtle, and none of us will do this exactly right, but I just want to bring up this idea, and I hope it's helpful.
The path of healing and the path of transformation.
Probably at different points in our life and our practice arc, one or the other is more important, and that may shift back and forth, actually.
That's sometimes very upsetting to people.
I've known people like this.
They're gung-ho on the path of transformation and they practice so hard and they feel so, whatever, clear and light, and then some deep conditioning gets triggered and they're a sobbing mess.
Some of them end up quitting the practice, actually.
I knew somebody like that.
Because, like, what?
This thing doesn't work?
But then you've got to pivot to healing, to deep healing, and forget all that.
Forget about transformation.
Get nurtured.
So that's one little note stemming from my Oregon pilgrimage, and I'll think of other things maybe later on.
And I want to continue now with the project we've been embarking on on Wednesday nights this year, to unpack the chant book.

It's not a technique thing, transformation.
It's about immersion and familiarity and trust, learning to trust that which we don't understand in the way that the mind tries to understand.
So that's great.

So I want to share a little bit about the Hymn to the Perfection of Wisdom that we just got to chant.

*Hymn to the perfection of wisdom.
Homage to the perfection of wisdom.
The lovely, the holy.
The perfection of wisdom gives light.
Unstained, the entire world cannot stain her.
She is a source of light, and from everyone in the triple world she removes darkness.
The most excellent are her works.
She brings light so that all fear and distress may be forsaken, and disperses the gloom and darkness of delusion.
She herself is an organ of vision.
She has a clear knowledge of the own being of all dharmas, for she does not stray away from it.
The perfection of wisdom of the Buddhas, that's in motion, the wheel of dharma.*
Isn't that lovely?
Just lovely.
And most of it's pretty understandable.
A few parts are a little bit obscure.
This is the beginning of a chapter of a long sutra on the perfection of wisdom, on the prajnaparamita.
As you might have figured out by now, this prajnaparamita stuff is really important in our lineage.
We talked about it all through our series on the six paramitas on Sundays, all year.
It's the sixth one that makes all of them go.
And we chant the Heart Sutra every week, and we dedicate pretty much everything with the line "maha prajnaparamita."
Maha just means great.
So we're constantly saying, "Great paramita, great paramita."
That's exactly what we're saying, actually.
The prajnaparamita literature emerged around 100 or 200 before the common era as a way of really exploring this transformational quality of the teachings, the wisdom that goes beyond wisdom.
The Indian Buddhist pundits at the time were writers, poets.
They explored this in writing with great enthusiasm.

And we think the first text that they wrote, and who knows, it was one author or many authors, and of course, like all of the Buddhist texts that were written later, they always claim they were written by the Buddha, which religiously is absolutely true, historically not so much.
So the first one we think they wrote is this one, the Prajnaparamita in 8,000 lines.
That's how they named them, just by word count.
You probably wouldn't sell a lot of novels.
It was like a novel in 32,552 words.
That's how they titled these.
Nothing about the topic, while the topic is the perfection of wisdom.

And then after doing one that's 8,000 lines long, and not exactly lines, 8,000 verses, 8,000 verses long, they did one that's 25,000 verses long, and one that's 100,000 verses long, a great big thing.
And there was a scholar in the fifties and sixties, actually born in Germany, who lived in England and ended up in America, named Edward Konza.
For some reason he fell in love with this literature in Sanskrit, and he translated almost all of it, an incredible scholarly feat.
I know people who knew him, who had him as their professor when they were young and in college.
And this was translated by that particular person.
So it's just interesting to me how these things get to a new culture.

It's basically a long meditation on what it would be if we really felt and realized the empty nature of all that is, the way things aren't separate, the way they aren't like our concepts make them seem.
They're much more open and fluid and free than any of that.
And they're wonderful and kind of challenging to read, and you can imagine trying to read 100,000 verses on this.
I have not done that, but I've read most of this one.
And it mostly is dialogue.
So I want to read you a typical little section of it, and then I'll tell you about the part that led to our little hymn here and why I think our little hymn is important.
I'll read to you.
I'm kind of off-script here, yeah.
So it's mostly a dialogue between the Buddha and two of his disciples, Sabuddhi and Shariputra.
And you might recall, maybe, if you were around then, when we were talking about the Heart Sutra, there's a little frame story that tells us it too is a dialogue.
Although, in this case, the Buddha inspires the dialogue from meditation, and it's a dialogue between Shariputra, one of these same two monks, and Avalokiteshvara, the Bodhisattva of Compassion.
That's unique.
Most of the time the Bodhisattva of Compassion doesn't show up in these other ones, as far as I know, but the Buddha and his two disciples do show up.
So here's a little sample.
It'll wash over you, so don't try too hard to figure anything else.
In this particular moment, the Buddha's there, and Shariputra is talking, and a god shows up to join the dialogue, named Sakra.
So Sabuddhi's talking to Sakra.
*Sabuddhi then said to Sakra, Now, listen and attend well.
I will teach you how a Bodhisattva should stand in perfect wisdom.
Through standing in emptiness should he stand in perfect wisdom.
Should he stand in perfect wisdom.
Armed with the great armor, the Bodhisattva should so develop that she does not take her stand on any of these, not on form, not on feeling, not on perception, not on impulses, consciousness.*
Does that sound familiar?

*Not on eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, mind, not on form, smells, taste, touch, touchables, mind, objects, not on eye consciousness, etc., until we come to not on mind consciousness, etc., until we come to not on the elements, i.e. earth, water, fire, wind, ether, consciousness, not on the pillars of mindfulness, right efforts, or roads to psychic power, faculties, powers, limbs of enlightenment,*
These are all parts of Buddhism, limbs of the path.
*Not on the fruits of the stream winner, the once returner, the never returner, or arhatship, not on pratikabuddhahood, nor on Buddhahood.
She should not take her stand on the idea that this is form, etc.

She should not take her stand on the idea that form is permanent or impermanent, or that form is easeful or suffering, or that form is the self or not the self, or that form is lovely or repulsive, or that form is empty or apprehended as something.
He should not take his stand on the notion that the fruits of the holy life derive their dignity from the unconditioned.
No, Sakra.
The bodhisattva should stand only in perfect wisdom and only stand in emptiness.*
Got it?
It goes on like this for many, many, many pages, with lots of negation like you heard, and language like we heard some time ago when we were studying the Diamond Sutra in here, too.

Anyway, after they got to their peak, and the longest one we're aware of (there may be others that were lost) of a hundred thousand verses of this kind of stuff, exploring emptiness, exploring prajnaparamita, then they must have realized, man, nobody's going to read these.
So they wrote shorter ones.

They wrote the Diamond Sutra, and they wrote the Heart Sutra, which aren't exactly in verses, but it goes more or less down from a hundred thousand to like five hundred and thirty or something like that.
And anyway, in one of the chapters of this text, chapter seven, after lots and lots of tangled logic of emptiness like that, on and on and on, suddenly we break into praise.
And we have the text that was edited a little bit to make our little chant here, this hymn.
So it's a prayer, really.
It's a prayer that we will really understand emptiness, really love wisdom.
To make the prayer really work as a prayer, prajnaparamita can also be personified, and usually personified as a she.
Maybe a he or a they, I don't know, but the examples I know of are all of a she.
And this being, who is not exactly a person, and it's not exactly clear if they would be called the bodhisattva, but an emanation of wisdom in female form, gives us something to focus on, right?
Someone to be with, and someone to relate to and love.
And as you heard there, this being, this emanation of wisdom, is lovely, is holy, gives light, and can't be blemished.
She doesn't have any faults, doesn't get caught by anything.
And like the bodhisattva of compassion, and there's a close connection here for sure, her whole deal is to bring light and healing, and to remove darkness.
You just hear that the emphasis is on wisdom, whereas with Avalokiteshvara, Kannon, Kanzeon, the emphasis is compassion.
And she does this so that we'll be free from fear, and free from darkness.
The key line in our little hymn is:
*She has a clear knowledge of the own being of all dharmas, for she does not stray away from it.*
Own being is a technical term, meaning what's the essence of things?
What's the nature of things?
What's their selfness?
And, of course, she knows that the own being of all dharmas is empty.
There's nothing solid to hold onto, there's nothing we can grasp, nothing we can make permanent.
There's only a shifting kaleidoscope of realities and textures and flavors as conditions change, and as everything co-arises according to the great cosmic wheel of karma.
Things are not not real, but they're just not real in that fixed way we tend to think they are, which then leads us to be upset when they change, such as being alive, for instance.
That's going to change.
So she can see that, and the beautiful part here is where it says, "for she does not stray away from it."
So this doesn't freak her out, you know?
She's comfortable and content with the way things actually are.
And because of that, she can set in motion the wheel of dharma, which has been turning since the beginning of time, so that we can all practice.
So this is a lovely addition.
I'm so glad we usually chant this after the Heart Sutra, because it helps us see this isn't just stuff to think about or figure out.
These are teachings to love.
Teachings to hold close.
Teachings to appreciate in our bones.

To sing for.
